title: Standing, at rest
desc: Standing figure at rest, seen from the front. Feet about hip-width apart and turned out slightly, weight even across both legs, spine vertical, shoulders level and loose, arms hanging at the sides with relaxed, softly curled hands. Nothing here is a message; it is a reference line.

annotations.text: Shoulders level and low: the resting line you measure from

title: Weight on one leg
desc: Standing figure with its weight settled on its left leg. The left hip rides higher, the right knee is soft and the right foot rests slightly forward and out, and the shoulders tilt gently the other way. A common, comfortable resting posture; for many people this is the baseline, not a sign of anything.

title: Open and settled
desc: Standing figure, feet shoulder-width apart, weight even, spine tall without stiffness, shoulders broad and relaxed, arms hanging a little away from the body with palms turned slightly forward. Reads as unguarded and at ease, in this person, in this moment.

annotations.text: Shoulders down and wide, not pinned back

title: Arms folded, loose
desc: Standing figure with its arms folded loosely across the lower chest, the left forearm resting over the right, hands relaxed and partly tucked. Shoulders are low, weight rests slightly on the left leg, the head is level. For many people this is simply how they stand when they are cold, tired, or comfortable.

annotations.text: A low, loose fold: forearms resting, not gripping

title: Arms folded, gripping
desc: Standing figure with its arms crossed high and tight across the chest, the left hand gripping the right upper arm. Both shoulders are lifted about two centimetres toward the ears, the feet are close together and the chin is slightly lowered. Compared with a loose fold, the difference is muscle effort: the grip and the lift, not the crossing itself.

annotations.text: The hand grips the upper arm
Shoulders lifted about 2 cm above their resting line

title: Hands in pockets
desc: Standing figure with both hands in the front trouser pockets, elbows slightly out, weight resting a little on the left leg, shoulders easy. A habitual resting posture for many people. It hides the hands, which matters to an observer only if it is a change from how this person usually stands.

title: Shoulders raised
desc: Standing figure with both shoulders drawn up toward the ears by several centimetres, arms held close to the sides, hands loosely curled, feet close. The neck looks shorter. A posture of bracing: it often appears under cold, strain, or uncertainty, and it is easy to hold for minutes without noticing.

annotations.text: Shoulder raised above its resting line: this is the tell

title: Collapsed through the chest
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters, upper back rounded forward, chest hollowed, shoulders rolled in, head carried forward of the chest with the chin dropped. Arms hang slightly in front of the body. Reads as depleted or withdrawn, or as someone who has spent nine hours at a laptop. The posture alone cannot tell you which.

annotations.text: Head carried ahead of the chest

title: Upright, in profile
desc: Standing figure in profile, facing right. Ear, shoulder, hip and ankle stack roughly on one vertical line; the chest is open without being puffed, the chin is level, the arms hang at the sides. This is a stacked posture, not a military one, and it costs little effort to hold.

title: Slumped, in profile
desc: Standing figure in profile, facing right. The upper back curves forward, the shoulders roll ahead of the chest, and the head juts forward and down so the ear sits well in front of the shoulder. The arms hang slightly forward. Compared with the stacked profile, the head alone has travelled several centimetres.

annotations.text: Ear well ahead of the shoulder

title: Hand to the throat
desc: Standing figure touching the front of its neck: the left hand lies flat across the hollow at the base of the throat, fingers pointing toward the right collarbone, elbow down. The other arm hangs at the side. Covering this hollow is one of the most commonly reported self-soothing touches. It says that something has registered, not what.

annotations.text: The hand covers the hollow at the base of the throat
Elbow kept close to the body

title: Rubbing the back of the neck
desc: Standing figure with its right hand behind its head, the palm cupping and rubbing the back of the neck, elbow raised and forward. The head is tipped slightly forward. A self-soothing touch that often follows a difficult question, a mistake, or a moment of embarrassment, and also a stiff neck.

annotations.text: Palm on the back of the neck

title: Fingers to the cheek
desc: Standing figure with the fingertips of its left hand resting against the left cheek and jaw, elbow pointing down, head tilted a few degrees toward the hand. Face touching is extremely common, many times an hour in ordinary adults, so its meaning lives entirely in its timing and in how far it departs from that person's usual rate.

title: Hands wringing
desc: Standing figure with both hands clasped in front of the stomach, fingers interlaced and pressing against each other, elbows bent and held close, shoulders slightly raised. Hand-to-hand rubbing and wringing is a self-soothing pattern. At rest it can also be the habit of someone who does not know where to put their hands.

annotations.text: Hands pressing and turning against each other

title: Holding one's own arm
desc: Standing figure with its left arm across the front of the body, the left hand holding the right upper arm just above the elbow, the right arm hanging close. A partial barrier and a self-hold at once. Common in people waiting alone in public, and in moments of exposure or uncertainty.

annotations.text: The hand holds the opposite arm

title: Hands on hips
desc: Standing figure with both hands on its hips, fingers forward, elbows pointing out to the sides, feet set wide. It takes up horizontal space. People adopt it to rest, to assert, to wait for a decision, or because their back aches. The stance is common; the reason is not visible.

annotations.text: Elbows out: the body claims width

title: Speaking with open hands
desc: Standing figure gesturing while speaking: both forearms raised in front of the body at waist height, the left palm turned up, the right hand open and angled inward, as if shaping an idea. Gestures like these, called illustrators, rise and fall with fluent speech.

title: Head tilted, listening
desc: Standing figure with its head tilted to its left by about ten degrees and turned slightly, as if listening, arms relaxed at the sides, weight resting on the left leg. A head tilt during listening is often read as interest. It can also be fatigue, a stiff neck, or a habit, which is why it needs this person's baseline.

title: Gaze lowered
desc: Standing figure with its chin lowered and its head pitched forward about twenty-five degrees, so the gaze falls to the floor a metre or so ahead. Shoulders are level, arms relaxed. People lower their gaze to think, to remember, to defer, to grieve, or because they are reading their phone.

title: Turned toward the exit
desc: Standing figure whose feet and hips point away to its right while the head and shoulders stay partly turned toward the viewer, as though still talking while already leaving. When the head stays and the feet go, the lower body may be ahead of the conversation, or the person may simply be waiting for a bus.

annotations.text: Both feet angled toward the exit

title: Still, held
desc: Standing figure held unusually still: arms pinned straight against the sides, hands flat against the thighs, feet together, shoulders slightly raised, head level and fixed. The stillness is the signal. A sudden reduction of ordinary movement often accompanies heavy thinking or a moment of alarm.

annotations.text: Hands stopped, pressed to the thighs

title: Seated, at rest
desc: Seated figure on a straight-backed chair, back resting lightly against it, feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart, knees bent at roughly a right angle, hands resting on the thighs. The seated reference posture: nothing in it is a signal.

title: Leaning in
desc: Seated figure leaning well forward from the hips, forearms resting on the knees, hands hanging loosely between them, head raised so the gaze stays fixed ahead. Close attention. In a conversation it can read as warm engagement; aimed at a stranger who did not invite it, it reads as scrutiny.

annotations.text: The trunk inclined toward the other person

title: Heel lifted, bouncing
desc: Seated figure with its left heel raised off the floor on the ball of the foot, as in a repetitive leg bounce; the right foot is flat. Hands rest on the thighs. Leg bouncing is one of the most frequent seated habits: for one person it is restlessness, for another spare energy, for a third simply how they sit.

title: Ankles locked under the chair
desc: Seated figure with its ankles crossed and pulled back beneath the chair, hands gripping the front edge of the seat, shoulders slightly raised, back held away from the chair. The body is braced as if waiting for something. People sit like this in waiting rooms, on first dates, and in the opening minutes of interviews.

annotations.text: Ankles hooked and withdrawn under the seat

title: Leaning back, expansive
desc: Seated figure leaning back into the chair, one arm draped over the chair back, the other hand resting on its thigh, legs apart with the left ankle crossed onto the right knee. The body takes up a great deal of room. Comfortable, or performing comfort; posture alone cannot say which.

annotations.text: Arm draped over the chair back
Ankle on knee: a wide, open lap

title: Chin in hand
desc: Seated figure leaning slightly forward, left elbow lowered toward the knee, chin resting on the loosely curled left hand, gaze forward. The other hand rests on the thigh. A thinking posture for many people and a tired one for others; as a habit it says almost nothing until it changes.

title: Seated, hand to the neck
desc: Seated figure that has just raised its left hand to the front of its neck, fingers spread across the base of the throat, elbow down; the right hand stays on the thigh. Seen alone, it is a touch. Seen two seconds after a specific question, in someone who rarely touches their neck, it is a pointer worth noting.

annotations.text: The hand arrives at the throat

title: Folded in
desc: Seated figure folded forward over itself: upper back rounded, shoulders rolled in, arms wrapped around the body, head lowered, feet tucked back under the chair. The body is made smaller. Seen in grief, cold, exhaustion and pain, and sometimes in deep concentration on a phone held in the lap.

title: Hands still in the lap
desc: Seated figure upright, back clear of the chair, hands clasped quietly in the lap, knees and feet close together, head level. Composed. This can be calm, or it can be a person holding themselves very deliberately still; the difference shows only against how they sat before.

title: Planted, wide
desc: Standing figure with the feet set wider than the shoulders and planted flat, knees soft, arms loose at the sides, spine upright. A stable base that claims floor space. People stand like this when they feel secure, when they are bracing for confrontation, and when a long day has made their back ache.

annotations.text: A base wider than the shoulders

title: Feet together, made small
desc: Standing figure with the feet together, arms held close against the sides, shoulders slightly raised and rounded, head a little lowered. The body occupies as little floor as it can. It can belong to someone shy, cold, deferential, or simply standing in a crowded lift.

title: Standing, ankles crossed
desc: Standing figure with the weight on the right leg and the left foot crossed in front of it at the ankle, hands in pockets. A crossed stance is hard to hold if you need to move quickly, so observers often read it as comfort; people also adopt it out of habit or to ease a sore hip.

annotations.text: One ankle crossed in front of the other

title: At rest, three-quarter
desc: The standing reference figure turned three-quarters to the viewer: feet hip-width, weight even, arms hanging, spine vertical. From this angle, rounding of the shoulders and lean of the trunk become visible in a way they are not from the front.

annotations.text: Shoulders level, neither rolled nor pinned

title: At rest, in profile
desc: The standing reference figure in profile, facing right, with ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly stacked and the arms hanging naturally. Use it as the line against which leaning, slumping and bracing in profile are measured.

title: At rest, from behind
desc: The standing reference figure seen from behind: feet hip-width, arms at the sides, shoulders level. From behind, the line of the shoulders and the angle of the head carry most of what can be seen, which is why people so often read mood in a back turned to them.

annotations.text: The shoulder line carries the mood

title: Up on the toes
desc: Standing figure lifted onto the balls of both feet with the hands clasped behind the back, caught mid-rock from heel to toe. Rocking like this appears in waiting, impatience, pleasure and boredom alike; only its timing and this person's habits can separate them.

title: Hands behind the back
desc: Standing figure with both hands clasped behind the back at the base of the spine, chest open, weight even. Common in people inspecting something, waiting patiently or holding authority in a room. It also hides the hands completely, which in another person may be modesty, habit, or cold fingers.

annotations.text: Front of the body left open

title: Hands clasped low
desc: Standing figure with both hands loosely clasped in front of the hips, elbows relaxed, shoulders level. A waiting posture at ceremonies, in queues and in group photographs. It shields the front of the body a little and gives the hands somewhere to be.

title: One hand in a pocket
desc: Standing figure with the left hand in a trouser pocket and the right forearm raised in an easy gesture, weight resting on the left leg. A relaxed speaking posture for many people: one hand engaged, the other parked.

annotations.text: The other hand parked in a pocket

title: Arms folded, in profile
desc: Standing figure seen in profile, facing right, with the arms folded across the chest. From the side the forearms stack in front of the ribs like a shelf, and you can see whether the shoulders are lifted or resting. Here they rest.

annotations.text: Forearms folded in front of the ribs

title: One hand on the hip
desc: Standing figure with the left hand resting on the hip, elbow out, weight settled on the left leg and the right knee soft. A casual, half-open stance seen in conversation and in waiting, and in anyone whose lower back is tired.

annotations.text: One elbow out to the side

title: Holding one's own wrist
desc: Standing figure with the left hand gripping the right wrist in front of the body, arms low. Holding your own wrist is a quiet mix of restraint and comfort: at a funeral it reads as composure, in a meeting it may be nerves, and in many people it is simply where the hands go.

annotations.text: One hand holding the other wrist

title: Hand over the mouth
desc: Standing figure with the left hand raised across the mouth, fingers along the cheek, elbow down. People cover the mouth when shocked, when thinking before speaking, when holding back a laugh or a word, and when they cough. The timing carries the meaning; the hand alone does not.

title: Hand over the eyes
desc: Standing figure with the left hand covering the eyes and the head tipped slightly forward. A gesture of blocking out, seen in grief, embarrassment, exhaustion and disbelief, and also in someone with a headache or tired eyes after hours at a screen.

title: Rubbing the forehead
desc: Standing figure with the fingertips of the right hand pressed to the forehead and the head bowed slightly into the touch. A common self-soothing and thinking gesture that often accompanies effortful recall, a mistake, a long day, or a headache.

title: Scratching the head
desc: Standing figure with the right hand at the side of the head, fingers in the hair, elbow raised. In cartoons it means puzzlement; in life it is just as often an itch, a habit, or a way to fill a pause while thinking.

title: Fingers at the collar
desc: Standing figure with the right hand at the side of the neck, fingers tugging at the collar. Adjusting the collar is a classic self-touch that can rise with heat, embarrassment or strain, and also with a tight shirt.

title: Stroking a forearm
desc: Standing figure with the left hand stroking the right forearm, which hangs close to the body. Slow, repeated stroking of the arm soothes, and it appears in waiting rooms and difficult conversations, as well as in someone who is simply cold.

title: Palms down the thighs
desc: Seated figure leaning slightly forward with both palms pressed flat on the thighs, as if sliding them toward the knees. The movement wipes damp palms and settles the body at once; it often comes just before speaking, standing up, or answering something difficult.

title: Seated, rubbing the jaw
desc: Seated figure with the left hand rubbing along the jaw and the right hand resting on the thigh. Rubbing and stroking the jaw shows up while weighing a decision and while hearing something unwelcome, and in people who simply have stubble to rub.

title: Direct gaze
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters, head level and facing straight ahead, with the line of gaze drawn. Direct gaze holds attention in many cultures and reads as a challenge in others. How long it lasts, and whether it is returned, matters more than the gaze itself.

title: Glance aside
desc: Standing figure with the body facing forward and the head turned about forty degrees to its left, gaze following. A glance aside can be distraction, a check on a sound, a wish to leave, or a break from eye contact that lets someone think.

title: Gaze down and away
desc: Standing figure with the head turned to its right and dropped, gaze falling to the floor off to one side. People look down and away when remembering, feeling ashamed, deferring, or giving someone room; studies of gaze aversion find it rises with mental effort.

annotations.text: Gaze to the floor, off to one side

title: Gaze raised
desc: Standing figure with the chin lifted and the gaze raised above eye level, slightly to one side, as many people do while recalling or composing something. Popular claims that the direction of an upward glance shows lying or truth-telling have not held up when tested.

title: Looking over the shoulder
desc: Standing figure seen from behind, body facing away, head turned far over the left shoulder to look back. The body is going one way and attention another: a backward glance on leaving, a check behind, or a name called from across a room.

annotations.text: Head turned back over the shoulder

title: Chin raised
desc: Standing figure in profile with the chin lifted so the face tilts upward and the throat is exposed. A raised chin is read as pride or defiance in some settings and as attention to someone taller in others. It is also how people look at a screen through the lower half of their glasses.

title: Chin tucked
desc: Standing figure in profile with the chin drawn down and back toward the chest, eyes looking out from under the brow. A tucked chin protects the throat and is common in uncertainty, cold and concentration; it is also a posture correction many people practise on purpose.

title: The bottom of a nod
desc: Standing figure caught at the low point of a nod, chin dropped toward the chest, seen at three-quarters. Nods regulate a conversation: slow single nods often mean go on, quick repeated ones often mean I have it, move along. Their meaning depends on culture and on the person's usual rhythm.

title: Braced upright
desc: Standing figure in profile held stiffly upright: chest pushed forward, shoulders pulled hard back, chin tucked, arms pinned to the sides. Compared with an easy stacked posture it costs visible effort, and it is common in people trying to look composed under scrutiny.

title: Hanging on the hips
desc: Standing figure in profile with the hips pushed forward and the upper body leaning back over them, upper back rounded. Sometimes called sway-back, it is a low-effort way to stand when tired, and to someone who does not know the person it can look like nonchalance or disengagement.

title: Leaning in, standing
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters, leaning forward from the hips with one foot slightly ahead, as if drawn toward a speaker. Leaning toward someone often goes with interest; it also happens in noisy rooms and with listeners who are hard of hearing.

title: Leaning away, standing
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters with the weight shifted onto the back foot and the trunk leaning slightly away. Leaning back can mark doubt, distaste or a wish for more room; it is also what people do to take in something large, or to get out of the way of someone's coffee.

annotations.text: Weight moving to the rear foot

title: Drawn in
desc: Standing figure drawn in on itself: arms wrapped tightly across the chest, shoulders raised and rounded, head down, feet together. The body takes up as little space as it can. Cold, fear, shame and fatigue can all produce it; so can a crowded train.

title: Pointing
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters with the right arm extended and the index finger pointing ahead. Pointing directs attention efficiently; pointing at a person is rude or aggressive in many cultures, where an open hand or a tilt of the head is used instead.

title: Palm down, settling
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters with the right forearm out at waist height and the palm turned down, as in a settling or slowing gesture. Palm-down gestures often go with firm statements or requests to calm down; whether they feel reassuring or dismissive depends on the relationship and the tone.

title: Shrug
desc: Standing figure in a full shrug: shoulders raised, forearms out to the sides with the palms turned up, head tilted. A shrug usually says some version of I don't know or what can you do. A half shrug of one shoulder can slip out while someone states something they are unsure of.

title: Edge-of-hand emphasis
desc: Standing figure with the right forearm raised and the hand held flat and upright like a blade, as if cutting the air to mark a point. A beat gesture that rises with emphasis; speakers use it to separate items and to signal certainty.

title: Waving hello
desc: Standing figure with the right arm raised beside the head, elbow bent, palm open and forward, as in a wave. Waves differ from place to place, side to side, up and down, palm in; in some countries a palm-out wave also means no.

title: Hand raised high
desc: Standing figure with the right arm raised straight up, palm forward, as in asking to speak or volunteering. The height of a raised hand often tracks urgency or confidence; a hand lifted only to the shoulder is the hesitant version.

title: Steepled hands, standing
desc: Standing figure with the fingertips of both hands pressed together in front of the chest, forming a steeple. Popular books call steepling a sign of confidence. In practice it is a common thinking and listening posture that tells you little until you know how often this person uses it.

title: Arms wide
desc: Standing figure with both arms swept out wide in front, palms up, as in describing something large or welcoming someone. Wide gestures tend to grow with enthusiasm and with the size of the room, and they vary a great deal between cultures and individuals.

title: Legs crossed at the knee
desc: Seated figure with the left leg crossed over the right at the knee, the left foot hanging free, hands resting on the thighs. One of the commonest ways to sit in many Western settings. In parts of the Middle East and Southeast Asia, showing someone the sole of your foot is an insult.

annotations.text: The sole of the crossed foot

title: Ankle on knee, upright
desc: Seated figure, upright, with the left ankle resting on the right knee and that knee out to the side, hands on the thighs. The so-called figure four takes up room and is common among men in relaxed settings; in formal or cross-cultural ones it can read as too casual.

title: Hands behind the head
desc: Seated figure leaning back with the fingers laced behind the head and the elbows spread wide, legs apart. It can be ease, a stretch after sitting too long, or a show of being unbothered. Who else is in the room usually decides how it lands.

title: Perched on the edge
desc: Seated figure perched toward the front of the chair, back held clear of it, heels slightly lifted and hands on the thighs, as if ready to stand. Perching appears in eagerness and impatience, in people about to leave, and in those who were never offered a comfortable chair.

title: Slouched low
desc: Seated figure slid low in the chair, legs stretched out, back rounded, head sunk toward the chest. Slouching can be fatigue, boredom, comfort among friends, or a long day. To a teacher or an interviewer it often reads as disrespect, which is a judgment about norms, not about the person.

title: Turned toward a neighbour
desc: Seated figure with the hips facing forward but the shoulders and head turned about thirty degrees to its left, as if toward someone in the next seat. How much of the body turns toward a person, and how quickly, is one of the clearer signs of where attention is going.

title: Hugging a knee
desc: Seated figure with the left foot drawn up onto the seat and both arms wrapped around the raised knee, chin lowered toward it. A gathering, self-holding posture common in teenagers and in tired or sad adults, and also simply a comfortable way to sit at home.

title: Head down to a phone
desc: Seated figure with the head dropped forward and the gaze on a phone held in both hands above the lap, shoulders slightly rounded. Phone posture now accounts for much of what looks like withdrawal or low mood in public places; check what the hands are doing before reading the head.

title: Walking
desc: Figure in profile mid-stride: left foot forward and planted, right heel lifting behind, arms swinging opposite the legs. The reference walk. Pace, stride length and arm swing vary widely with height, age, footwear and mood.

annotations.text: Front heel down, back heel lifting

title: Brisk walk
desc: Figure in profile in a long, brisk stride with a slight forward lean and a full arm swing. A brisk walk often reads as purpose or confidence; it is also simply what people do when they are late.

title: Slow walk, head down
desc: Figure in profile taking a short step with the head down, shoulders rounded and the arms hanging without swinging. Pace slows and arm swing shrinks with fatigue, pain, low mood and age; a single walk cannot tell you which.

title: Walking, hands in pockets
desc: Figure seen at three-quarters walking with both hands in the trouser pockets. Pocketed hands remove the arm swing, which can make a walk look guarded or casual depending on the rest of the body, the weather and the person.

title: Walking, eyes on a phone
desc: Figure in profile walking slowly with a phone held up in the right hand and the head bent toward it. Studies of pedestrians find that people texting while they walk slow down, shorten their steps and drift off a straight line.

title: Walking toward you
desc: Figure walking straight toward the viewer, left foot forward, arms swinging opposite. Seen head-on, a walk shows mostly its width: how far apart the feet track and how much the shoulders roll.

title: Easy breath
desc: Standing figure in profile breathing easily: belly soft and slightly forward, chest quiet, shoulders down. Relaxed breathing at rest is mostly diaphragmatic and moves the abdomen more than the upper chest.

annotations.text: Belly soft, moving with the breath

title: Breathing high in the chest
desc: Standing figure in profile drawing breath high into the chest: chest lifted and expanded, shoulders rising, belly held in. Shoulder-lifting breaths often come with anxiety, exertion and effortful speech, and some people breathe this way out of habit.

title: Breathing low into the belly
desc: Standing figure in profile breathing low: the abdomen swells forward on the in-breath while the chest and shoulders stay still. Slow abdominal breathing is the basis of most breathing practices used to lower arousal.

title: Breath held
desc: Standing figure in profile with the chest held full and still, shoulders slightly raised and arms close: the posture of a held breath. People hold their breath when concentrating, bracing for news and in moments of fright; the release, when it comes, is often a visible sigh.

title: Long exhale
desc: Standing figure in profile at the end of a long out-breath: chest sunk, shoulders dropped, upper back softening forward, head bowed a little. A long exhale can be relief, resignation or deliberate calming; after a held breath it usually marks a release of tension.

title: Face in the hands
desc: Seated figure folded forward, elbows near the knees, face buried in both hands. A posture of overwhelm, common in grief and despair, and also in exhaustion and intense concentration. If you see it in someone you know, the right response is to sit nearby and ask, not to interpret.

title: Standing, head bowed
desc: Standing figure with the head deeply bowed, chin toward the chest, hands clasped low in front. A posture seen at gravesides, memorials and moments of silence, where it is both private feeling and public ritual.

title: Kneeling, head bowed
desc: Kneeling figure seen at three-quarters, upright on both knees, hands resting on the thighs, head bowed low. Kneeling marks prayer, mourning and reverence in many traditions; it is also how people tend a grave or speak to someone sitting on the ground.

title: Folded forward, in profile
desc: Seated figure in profile folded forward over the knees, arms wrapped around the body, head down. From the side you can see how far the trunk has collapsed toward the lap: a protective shape that grief, nausea, cold and exhaustion all produce.

title: Standing, arms around the body
desc: Standing figure with both arms wrapped around the body at the ribs, shoulders hunched, head down, feet close. A self-holding posture common in grief and shock, and also in someone standing outside in the cold.

title: Presenting, open
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters, presenting: one forearm raised with the palm up toward an audience, the other arm relaxed, weight even. Open-handed gesture while speaking tends to read as candour; its absence reads as nothing at all, since many good speakers barely gesture.

title: At the lectern
desc: Standing figure behind a lectern, hands resting on its slanted top, leaning slightly toward it. A lectern hides most of the body and gives the hands a place to hold; under nerves, a white-knuckled grip on its edges is common.

title: On a video call
desc: Seated figure in profile at a table facing a laptop, forearms resting on the tabletop, upright and close to the screen. On camera the shoulders, head and hands are almost all that can be read, and the angle of the camera does much of the reading for you.

title: Slumped at the laptop
desc: Seated figure in profile hunched toward a laptop: upper back rounded, shoulders rolled forward, head pushed out toward the screen. The posture of a long working day. It reads as tired or disengaged on camera, and it is mostly the furniture's fault.

title: Checking the time
desc: Standing figure with the left forearm raised across the body and the head bent to look at a watch. A glance at the time during a conversation is often taken as a wish to leave; it can also be a train to catch or a reminder to take medicine.

annotations.text: Wrist turned up toward the eyes

title: Taking notes
desc: Seated figure at a table leaning forward with the head down, the right hand writing and the left resting on the page. Note-taking breaks eye contact for long stretches; most speakers read it as attention, though some read it as a record being kept against them.

title: Listening at the table
desc: Seated figure at a table leaning in a little with the forearms on the tabletop and the head tilted, as in listening. Listening postures vary so much between people that a change from someone's own baseline matters far more than any of these features.

title: Arms folded, leaning back
desc: Seated figure at a table leaning back away from it with the arms folded across the chest. In a meeting this is often read as resistance; it is just as likely to be someone cold, someone tired, or someone listening comfortably.

title: A light bow
desc: Standing figure in profile bowing lightly from the hips, about fifteen degrees, back straight and arms at the sides. In Japan a bow of this depth, the eshaku, is an everyday greeting between equals; depth, duration and who bows first all carry meaning there.

annotations.text: Bending from the hips, back straight

title: A formal bow
desc: Standing figure in profile in a deeper, formal bow of about thirty degrees from the hips, back straight, arms at the sides, gaze lowered. In Japanese etiquette a bow of this depth, the keirei, shows respect in business and toward seniors.

annotations.text: A deeper bend, about thirty degrees

title: The wai
desc: Standing figure with the palms pressed together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, and the head bowed slightly toward them. In Thailand this is the wai: the higher the hands and the deeper the bow, the more respect shown, and the junior person is expected to offer it first.

title: Palms together, raised high
desc: Standing figure with the palms pressed together and raised to the level of the face, head bowed into them. Hands held this high signal deep respect: in Thailand they are raised this way toward monks and elders, and in Indian greetings toward someone especially honoured.

title: Hand on the heart
desc: Standing figure with the right hand placed flat over the heart and the head inclined. In many Muslim-majority and Middle Eastern settings this accompanies or replaces a handshake, and it is a respectful way to greet someone who does not shake hands with people of another gender.

title: Gaze lowered in respect
desc: Standing figure with the head slightly inclined and the gaze held below the other person's eyes, hands clasped low. In many cultures, including communities in East and South Asia, West Africa and many Indigenous nations, avoiding a direct gaze toward an elder or senior is a mark of respect, not evasion.

title: Resting squat
desc: Figure resting in a deep squat with the heels flat on the ground, forearms on the knees and hands hanging between them. An ordinary way to rest, wait or talk across much of Asia, Africa and the Middle East; observers unused to it sometimes misread it as loitering.

title: A raised palm across a room
desc: Standing figure with the right hand lifted briefly to shoulder height, palm forward, chin raised: a small acknowledgement to someone across a room. Low-cost greetings like this keep acquaintances warm without requiring a conversation.

title: On one knee
desc: Figure down on the left knee with the right foot planted in front, forearm resting on the raised knee, trunk upright. Taking a knee brings an adult down to a child's eye level or to someone sitting on the ground; it is also how people tie a shoe.

title: Face to face, at a conversational distance
desc: Two standing figures in profile facing each other a little over a metre apart, both at rest. This is about where Edward Hall placed the boundary between personal and social distance for conversation among acquaintances in the United States; comfortable distances vary widely by culture, relationship and setting.

title: Too close
desc: Two figures in profile standing less than half a metre apart. The one on the right leans in; the one on the left leans back with the weight on the rear foot and the chin drawn away. When someone enters space another person treats as intimate, the usual response is to restore distance with the body by leaning, stepping back or turning.

title: Side by side
desc: Two standing figures side by side, a forearm's length apart, both facing forward toward something ahead of them. Many men find it easier to talk side by side, walking, driving or watching something, than face to face, where a steady mutual gaze can feel like scrutiny.

title: An open angle
desc: Two standing figures at roughly a right angle to each other, both turned toward a point between them, like the sides of an open letter L. Angled positions allow conversation with less unbroken eye contact than face to face, and they leave room for a third person to join.

title: Handshake
desc: Two standing figures in profile shaking right hands, about three-quarters of a metre apart, each arm extended to meet in the middle. Grip, length, distance and whether the other hand joins in vary across cultures and people; a firm grip is prized in some places and seen as aggressive in others.

title: Embrace
desc: Two figures in profile in a full embrace, chests close, one arm over the other's shoulder and one around the back. Hugs between men often come with back slaps that keep them brief; a long, still embrace usually marks something larger, such as grief or a reunion.

title: An arm around the shoulders
desc: Two figures seen from behind standing side by side, one with an arm across the other's shoulders while the other's head is bowed. A side embrace is a common form of comfort and solidarity between men; it can be easier to accept than a hug because neither has to face the other.

annotations.text: Hand resting on the far shoulder

title: Across a table
desc: Two seated figures in profile facing each other across a table, both leaning in a little with the forearms on the tabletop. A table sets the distance and puts a barrier between bodies, which is part of why interviews and negotiations feel more formal than the same conversation on a sofa.

title: Side by side on a bench
desc: Two figures seated side by side on a bench: one upright with the hands on the thighs, the other leaning forward with forearms on the knees and head down. Sitting beside someone, rather than across from them, is how a lot of men's hardest conversations happen.

annotations.text: Head down, forearms on the knees

title: At a child's height
desc: An adult down on one knee facing a young child, so that their heads are at about the same height. Coming down to a child's eye level makes a conversation less looming; it is one of the simplest things a parent, teacher or coach can do with the body.

title: A circle of three
desc: Three standing figures in a loose circle, turned toward a shared centre, with a gap left open on the near side. Conversational groups tend to arrange themselves like this, in what the linguist Adam Kendon called an F-formation, and whether the gap stays open or closes as someone approaches tells you how welcome a newcomer is.

title: Half out of the conversation
desc: Two figures in conversation. The one on the left faces the other fully. The one on the right keeps the head turned toward the conversation but has swung the feet and hips away, toward the room. When the lower body leaves before the head, a person may be ready to go, or may simply be waiting to be released politely.

title: The up-nod
desc: Standing figure seen at three-quarters with the chin flicked briefly upward and the head tipped back a few degrees, arms loose at the sides. Between men in many English-speaking places, a quick upward nod at a distance says I see you, often to an acquaintance; a downward nod is often the more formal or respectful version.

title: Fist bump
desc: Two standing figures in profile, each extending the right arm so that their closed fists meet in the middle at about chest height, a little more than an arm's length apart. A light, quick greeting that needs no grip and little closeness, common among friends, teammates and younger men.

title: The handshake pulled into a hug
desc: Two figures in profile, right hands still clasped between their chests while the left arms reach over each other's shoulders, bodies leaning in from the hips. The classic greeting between male friends: a grip that turns into a brief, half embrace, usually closed with a slap or two on the back.

annotations.text: A hand on the back, ready to pat

title: Side by side, arms across shoulders
desc: Two figures standing shoulder to shoulder and facing the same way, each with an arm across the other's shoulders and the free arm hanging loose. A side hug is common in photographs, at celebrations and among teammates; it offers closeness without either person having to face the other.

annotations.text: Hand resting on the far shoulder

title: A hand on the shoulder
desc: Two standing figures side by side at three-quarters: one rests a hand on the near shoulder of the other, whose head is bowed and shoulders rounded. A hand on the shoulder is among the most widely accepted forms of comfort between men; it asks for nothing and can be shrugged off easily.

title: Walking side by side
desc: Two figures walking side by side at a matched pace, seen at three-quarters, one with the head turned slightly toward the other as they talk. Walking together sets a shared rhythm and a shared direction, and many conversations that would stall across a table run easily on a walk.

annotations.text: A glance across, then back to the path

title: Working at the same bench
desc: Two figures standing side by side at a workbench, both leaning in with heads down and hands busy on the same job in front of them. Shared work gives two people somewhere to put their eyes and hands, and a lot of men's friendship is made in exactly this position.

annotations.text: Eyes on the work, not on each other

title: One leans in, one leans away
desc: Two standing figures in profile: one leans toward the other with a hand raised mid-gesture, while the other leans back from the hips, turns the shoulders away and folds the arms. Leaning away, turning and closing up are among the plainest signs that someone wants more distance, whatever the words are doing.

title: Coming to apologise
desc: Two standing figures in profile a little over an arm's length apart. One stands with a hand flat on the chest, head slightly lowered and the other hand open at the side; the other waits with arms folded and head turned a little away. An apology often has to be made to a body that is not yet ready to hear it.

title: Holding a baby
desc: Standing adult seen from the side, holding a small baby upright against the chest, one forearm under the baby's bottom and the other hand spread across its back, the baby's head resting near the shoulder. Supporting the head and neck matters in the first months, before a baby can hold its own head up.

annotations.text: A hand across the baby's back

title: A child on the hip
desc: Standing adult with a young child sitting on the left hip, one arm wrapped under the child's bottom, the hip pushed out to take the weight. Carrying a child on the hip leaves one hand free, and a hip shifted out like this is often the first sign of a parent across a room.

annotations.text: Hip out, taking the child's weight

title: Walking hand in hand with a child
desc: An adult and a young child walking side by side, seen at three-quarters, the adult's hand lowered and the child's arm lifted so that their hands meet between them. Walking with a small child means shortening the stride and lowering the hand to the child's height, not the other way round.

title: Showing a child how
desc: An adult down on one knee beside a young child, both facing the same way, the adult's near hand reaching toward the child's hands as both look down at the task in front of them. Teaching alongside, at the child's height, lets the child keep the job in their own hands.

annotations.text: The child's hands on the task

title: At the bedside
desc: A seated figure on a chair drawn up beside a bed, leaning forward with one hand reaching to hold the hand of the person lying there. Sitting down at the bedside, at the level of the person in the bed, changes the visit: it says that you are staying rather than passing through.

annotations.text: Holding the hand on the cover

title: Standing together, heads bowed
desc: Three figures standing in a row, facing the same way with heads bowed and hands clasped in front, one with an arm across the shoulders of the man beside him. Mourning together often looks like this: little speech, bodies close, attention on the same place.

title: Round a meeting table
desc: Five seated figures around a long meeting table: one at the head, two along one side, one along the other and one at the far end, hands resting on the table. Where people sit at a table shapes who speaks, who is spoken to and who is overlooked, often before the meeting has begun.

annotations.text: The far end, facing the head

title: Moving on a stage
desc: Standing presenter caught mid-step across a stage, one hand opening toward the audience palm up while the other swings naturally, head turned toward the room. Movement on a stage reads best when it has a purpose, such as walking to a new point for a new idea, rather than pacing.

annotations.text: An open hand toward the room

title: Too close to the camera
desc: Seated figure at a laptop leaning far forward from the hips, head pushed toward the screen, forearms on the table. On a video call this fills the frame with a face at the distance of a whisper, which many viewers find intense, and it usually means the person is straining to see or hear.

title: Joining a group
desc: A figure walking up to a loose circle of three, toward the side the group has left open; the two nearest members have turned toward him to make room. A group with an open side and members who turn to widen it is inviting a newcomer; a closed circle of backs is not.
